The Indian River Broiler (Gallus gallus IR) exhibits rapid early development, with a carefully documented incubation period. Eggs incubated at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] produce chicks that hatch precisely 21 days [ab = 21 days] after laying, a timing that is highly conserved across commercial broiler lines. Upon emergence, the wet weight of a neonate is consistently recorded at 39.6 grams [Wwb = 39.6 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves that sustain the chick through its first days of exogenous feeding. This initial mass is remarkably uniform within the strain, a characteristic that supports synchronized growth in commercial operations. The transition from yolk dependence to the first feeding on starter crumbles typically occurs within the first 24 hours post-hatch, marking the onset of the exotrophic phase. During this nestling stage, chicks are highly dependent on thermal regulation provided by the brooder environment, and their growth trajectory is strongly influenced by ambient temperature and feed access. The precise control of incubation temperature at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] is critical for normal organogenesis and for achieving the expected hatchling mass, which serves as a baseline for all subsequent growth performance metrics.

A key developmental milestone in the Indian River Broiler is the achievement of fledging, which under typical thermal conditions occurs at a specific duration after hatching. At the standard maintenance temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at fledging is recorded as 42 days since birth [tx = 42 days since birth], a value that was originally derived from the ancestral red junglefowl (Gallus gallus). This period marks the point at which the developing chick has attained full feathering and the ability to thermoregulate independently, effectively transitioning from a brooded nestling to a free-moving juvenile. The 42-day fledging age (42 days since birth) [tx = 42 days since birth] is a critical parameter for management schedules, as it signals the end of the intensive brooding phase at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. During this interval, the chick undergoes a rapid increase in body mass and skeletal development, driven by high-protein feed formulations designed to meet its metabolic demands. The environmental temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C] is maintained to optimize growth efficiency and minimize stress, which can cause mortality or reduced weight gain. This thermal condition is particularly important in the first two weeks of life, when the chick's own thermoregulatory capacity is still limited, and it directly influences the rate of feather development necessary for successful fledging.

Sexual maturation and the onset of reproductive capability in the Indian River Broiler show pronounced sexual dimorphism in their timing. At the operational temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], males reach the time since birth at puberty at 182 days since birth [tp = 182 days since birth], a stage marked by the onset of spermatogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics such as the comb and wattles. This value is derived from the time to first brood minus the typical clutch interval, reflecting the point at which physiological readiness for reproduction begins. In contrast, the time since birth at first brood for males is notably earlier, occurring at 90 days since birth [tR = 90 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], indicating that males are capable of successful mating before they have fully completed their own growth. Females, however, exhibit a markedly different schedule. Their first successful reproductive event, as measured by the time since birth at first brood, occurs at 189 days since birth [tR = 189 days since birth] when maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This later onset is consistent with the greater energetic demands of egg production and the need to achieve a sufficient body mass to support a clutch, highlighting a classic life-history trade-off between growth and reproduction.

Body mass at the onset of reproduction represents a critical life-history trait, and the Indian River Broiler exhibits clear sexual dimorphism in this parameter. At the point of their first successful brood, females achieve a wet weight of 2000 grams , a mass that balances the energetic costs of egg production with the need to maintain somatic condition. Males, on the other hand, reach their first breeding event at a substantially heavier mass of 2390 grams , a difference that likely reflects the competitive advantages of larger body size in male-male interactions for access to females. These weights are recorded under standard husbandry conditions and represent the minimum body condition necessary to initiate reproductive activity. Following the first brood, both sexes continue to grow, though at a decelerated rate, until they approach their ultimate body size. The ultimate wet weight for females in this strain is 4200 grams [Wwi = 4200 grams], while males asymptote at a significantly larger 5100 grams [Wwi = 5100 grams]. This striking sexual dimorphism in adult mass is a common feature in Gallus gallus lines selected for meat production, where males are preferentially bred for rapid growth and high final body weight.

The reproductive output and lifespan of the Indian River Broiler are tightly linked to its high metabolic rate and the thermal environment. Under the standard maintenance temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the maximum lifetime reproductive output is substantial, with breeders producing approximately 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 6 eggs per clutch] and achieving up to 52 clutches each year [F_R_i = up to 52 clutches each year]. This translates into an exceptionally high annual laying frequency, which is a product of intense artificial selection for egg production in the female line. However, this elevated reproductive effort comes at a cost to longevity. The maximum lifespan of the Indian River Broiler is 3650 days [am = 3650 days] when maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a duration that is considerably shorter than that of ancestral junglefowl, reflecting the trade-offs associated with rapid growth and high fecundity. Commercial breeders typically cull flocks well before they reach this potential lifespan, as egg quality and hatchability begin to decline after roughly two years of production. This maximum lifespan value (3650 days) [am = 3650 days] represents a theoretical upper bound under optimal, stress-free conditions, and it is rarely attained in commercial practice, where physiological exhaustion from sustained high output usually truncates life earlier at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C].
